The Case for Land Value Tax: Reclaiming the Commons for the Common Good

Introduction

Imagine a system of taxation that eliminates economic deadweight loss, reduces inequality, prevents housing speculation, discourages urban sprawl, and funds government entirely through capturing value that no individual created. This isn't utopian fantasy—it's the logical outcome of implementing a 100% land value tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land, as proposed by 19th-century political economist Henry George. By fully capturing land rent for public benefit, society can achieve both maximum economic efficiency and social justice while eliminating the need for taxes on labor, capital, and productive enterprise. The question isn't whether we can afford to implement comprehensive land value taxation—it's whether we can afford not to.

The Fundamental Injustice of Private Land Rent

The case for land value taxation begins with a simple ethical observation: land is fundamentally different from other forms of property. No human created land. Its value derives not from individual effort but from natural endowments, population density, public infrastructure, and the collective economic activity of communities. When a subway station opens, nearby land values soar—not because landowners improved their holdings, but because the public made an investment. When a neighborhood gentrifies due to community development, property values rise as a windfall to those who happened to hold title.

Current systems allow private individuals to capture this socially-created value as unearned income. A landowner who simply holds a vacant lot in a growing city becomes wealthy through no effort of their own, while workers who create actual value through labor see much of their wages taxed away. This represents a profound injustice: we tax people for what they contribute to society (labor and capital) while allowing them to privately capture what society contributes to land values.

Henry George identified this as the root cause of persistent poverty amid progress. As civilizations advance and productivity increases, land values rise accordingly. Rather than this increased wealth benefiting everyone, it concentrates in the hands of landowners, who extract an ever-growing tribute from the productive economy through rent. George called this "the unearned increment"—a toll on prosperity itself.

Economic Efficiency: The Only Tax That Improves Market Outcomes

From an economic efficiency standpoint, land value taxation is unparalleled. Standard economic theory teaches that most taxes create deadweight loss—they distort economic decisions, reducing overall welfare. Income taxes discourage work. Sales taxes discourage consumption. Capital gains taxes discourage investment. Each creates a wedge between the socially optimal level of activity and what actually occurs.

Land value taxation is the exception. Because the supply of land is perfectly inelastic—no amount of taxation can create more land—an LVT creates zero deadweight loss. Whether taxed at 1% or 100%, the same amount of land exists. This unique characteristic makes LVT what economists call "the perfect tax."

Moreover, LVT actively improves resource allocation. Under current systems, landowners can profit from speculation—buying land and holding it vacant or underutilized while waiting for values to appreciate. This withholding of land from productive use creates artificial scarcity, raising prices for everyone else. Major cities worldwide suffer from vacant lots, underused parcels, and "land banking" by speculators, even as housing shortages drive prices to unaffordable levels.

A full LVT eliminates the returns to speculation. When landowners must pay the full rental value of their land annually, holding vacant or underutilized land becomes expensive rather than profitable. This creates powerful incentives for efficient land use. Prime urban locations would naturally flow to their highest-value purposes—housing, businesses, and services that justify the tax obligation through productive use. The result: denser, more efficient cities with dramatically reduced sprawl and lower housing costs.

The Single Tax: Replacing All Other Taxes

George proposed that land rent could serve as the "single tax"—the sole source of government revenue. While this may sound radical, the mathematics are compelling. Studies suggest that total land rent in developed economies equals 15-30% of GDP, while government typically consumes 30-40% of GDP. At first glance, this appears insufficient.

However, this analysis misses several factors. First, current land values are suppressed by existing taxation regimes and underutilization. When land must be used productively due to LVT pressure, economic activity increases, raising land values substantially. Second, eliminating all other taxes would dramatically increase economic productivity—some economists estimate GDP could rise 20-25% or more without the drag of inefficient taxation. This expanded economy generates higher land rents. Third, much current government spending addresses problems that LVT would ameliorate or eliminate: housing subsidies become less necessary when housing is abundant; unemployment benefits decrease when job creation surges; economic development incentives become obsolete when efficient land use is automatic.

When these factors combine, capturing 100% of land rent could realistically fund government operations while allowing the complete elimination of:

  • Income taxes (personal and corporate)
  • Payroll taxes
  • Sales and VAT taxes
  • Capital gains taxes
  • Estate taxes
  • Business taxes

Imagine the economic dynamism of a society where no one pays taxes on their labor, investment, or enterprise—where the only public charge is for one's exclusive use of the commonwealth. Entrepreneurship would flourish, savings and investment would surge, and labor markets would tighten as artificial barriers to employment vanish.

Housing Affordability and Wealth Inequality

The housing affordability crisis plaguing major cities worldwide has a common root cause: land values that have risen far faster than incomes. In cities like San Francisco, Vancouver, London, and Sydney, ordinary workers are priced out of neighborhoods as land speculation drives costs to astronomical levels. The problem isn't construction costs—it's land costs.

LVT directly attacks this problem. By eliminating speculative returns, land prices would fall dramatically. When land cannot appreciate as a speculative asset, its price reflects only its current use value, not expected future windfalls. This could reduce land prices by 50-90%, making homeownership and business location affordable again. Meanwhile, the tax doesn't affect buildings or improvements—the same incentive structure that encourages efficient land use also encourages property improvement and development.

Similarly, LVT addresses wealth inequality at its source. The vast fortunes accumulated through real estate holdings often represent not entrepreneurial success but strategic land acquisition in locations that later became valuable through public investment and population growth. The wealthiest landowners are frequently descendants of those who secured titles generations ago through conquest, political connections, or simply being first. Their wealth represents the accumulated tribute extracted from everyone who came later.

By capturing land rent publicly, LVT prevents the transformation of socially-created value into privately-held, inheritable fortunes. This doesn't punish success—entrepreneurs and innovators still profit from their contributions. It simply ensures that value created by society benefits society.

Environmental and Urban Planning Benefits

The environmental case for LVT is powerful. Sprawl—the inefficient, low-density development pattern that characterizes much modern growth—is economically irrational but privately profitable under current systems. Developers can buy cheap rural land, build scattered developments, and leave the public to fund the infrastructure connecting them. Meanwhile, valuable urban land sits underutilized.

LVT reverses this logic. Low-value rural and agricultural land carries minimal tax burdens, making preservation economically sensible. High-value urban land faces strong pressure for efficient use, encouraging density and mixed-use development. The result: compact, walkable cities surrounded by preserved natural and agricultural land—precisely the pattern that minimizes environmental impact, reduces transportation emissions, and improves quality of life.

Transit-oriented development becomes automatic. Since land value increases most dramatically near transit stations, these locations face the highest LVT charges, creating maximum pressure for density exactly where it's most appropriate. No zoning mandates or developer incentives required—economic logic aligns perfectly with planning goals.

Simplicity and Transparency

Compared to current tax systems spanning thousands of pages of code with countless loopholes and exemptions, LVT is remarkably simple. Land can't be hidden in offshore accounts. Its value can be assessed through transparent methods based on comparable sales. No need to track income sources, monitor international transactions, or audit complex financial structures. Assessment becomes the primary administrative task, and regular reassessments ensure fairness.

This simplicity slashes compliance costs. Citizens and businesses need not hire accountants and lawyers to navigate Byzantine tax codes. No more tax preparation industry extracting billions in value while adding nothing productive. Enforcement becomes straightforward—property that hasn't paid its LVT can be identified immediately, and since land cannot be moved or hidden, collection is assured.

The transparency benefits democracy itself. Citizens can see exactly what they're paying and why—the publicly-assessed value of their land holding. No hidden payroll deductions, no VAT buried in prices, no corporate taxes camouflaged in product costs. This clarity enables informed political debate about public spending and revenue needs.

Addressing Practical Concerns

Critics raise several practical objections, but each has robust answers. The concern that elderly homeowners on fixed incomes couldn't afford LVT on appreciated property can be addressed through deferral programs, allowing tax obligations to accumulate as liens against eventual property transfer. Alternatively, since LVT dramatically lowers land prices initially, most homeowners would see total housing costs (purchase price plus tax) remain stable or decrease.

The transition challenge—how to shift from current systems to full LVT—can be managed gradually. Begin with a small LVT while proportionally reducing other taxes, then increase the rate over 10-20 years. This allows markets to adjust, prices to stabilize, and revenue systems to adapt. During transition, those who purchased land at inflated prices expecting continued appreciation do suffer capital losses, but this represents correction of an unjust windfall expectation, not creation of unfair hardship. Society shouldn't perpetuate inefficient systems to protect returns that were never economically justified.

The question of whether land rent truly suffices as a single tax is ultimately empirical and can be tested. Begin by funding specific government functions through LVT. As experience accumulates and land values adjust to the new incentive structure, the feasibility of full implementation becomes clearer. The direction is sound even if the ultimate endpoint requires adjustment.

The Moral Imperative

Beyond economics lies a fundamental moral argument. The earth wasn't created by any individual or generation—it is the common inheritance of humanity. Private property rights in the products of labor are just; individuals should own what they create through effort. But property rights in land itself represent a claim to monopolize what no one created and everyone needs.

Current systems allow some individuals to charge others for the privilege of existing on earth. Through no merit of their own, landowners collect tribute from those who must pay rent for homes, workspace, and business locations. This is morally indistinguishable from feudalism—a hereditary privileged class extracting value from the productive population simply by asserting exclusive control over necessary resources.

LVT restores the commons while preserving market efficiency. Private holders can still control specific land parcels and benefit from improvements they make, but they compensate the community for their exclusive use of a common resource. This aligns individual incentives with collective welfare: society benefits both from efficient private land use and from public capture of the value society itself created.

Conclusion

The case for 100% land value taxation is overwhelming on grounds of economic efficiency, social justice, environmental sustainability, and administrative simplicity. It would trigger profound positive changes: dramatically lower housing costs, increased economic growth, reduced inequality, efficient urban form, and simplified taxation. It would allow elimination of all economically damaging taxes on productive activity while funding government through capture of socially-created value that currently enriches landowners through no merit of their own.

The greatest puzzle about LVT isn't whether it would work—the theoretical and empirical evidence strongly support its benefits. The puzzle is why it hasn't been implemented. Perhaps entrenched interests of major landholders block reform. Perhaps the idea seems too simple, too elegant, to solve complex problems. Perhaps the initial transition costs deter political action despite enormous long-term benefits.

Whatever the barriers, they aren't intellectual. The arguments are sound. The question facing society is whether we have the wisdom to recognize them and the courage to act. Every day we delay represents continued injustice—continued taxation of productive labor while socially-created land values enrich private holders, continued housing affordability crises as speculation trumps use, continued economic inefficiency as perverse incentives distort resource allocation.

Henry George wrote that "the equal right of all men to use the land is as clear as their equal right to breathe the air." Land value taxation translates that moral insight into practical policy. It's time to reclaim the commons for the common good.

The Single Tax on Land Value: Justice, Efficiency, and the Path to True Prosperity

A Case for the Full Capture of Land Rent as the Sole Source of Public Revenue

Introduction

There exists in political economy a proposal so elegant in its logic, so profound in its justice, and so powerful in its consequences that its persistent neglect constitutes one of the great intellectual tragedies of modern civilization. That proposal is the 100% land value tax—the full public capture of the rental value of unimproved land as the single source of government revenue. First systematized by Henry George in his 1879 masterwork Progress and Poverty, and refined by generations of economists, philosophers, and reformers since, this idea strikes at the very root of inequality, inefficiency, and injustice in our economic order. It does not punish labor. It does not discourage investment. It does not distort markets. It simply returns to the community what the community has created: the value of land.

The argument for the full land value tax rests on three pillars—moral philosophy, economic efficiency, and practical governance—each of which, examined honestly, leads to the same inescapable conclusion. Private landownership, when it includes the privilege of pocketing land rent, is a form of legalized appropriation of communal wealth. A 100% tax on land's unimproved value corrects this injustice while simultaneously producing the most efficient, least distortionary, and most prosperous economic system achievable. This essay will argue each of these claims in turn, demonstrate why the land value tax should replace all other forms of taxation, and address the most common objections.

Part I: The Moral Case — Land Belongs to Everyone

The Distinction Between Land and Capital

The foundation of the Georgist argument rests on a distinction that classical economists understood clearly but that modern discourse has dangerously blurred: the categorical difference between land and capital. Capital—buildings, machinery, tools, inventory, intellectual property—is produced by human effort. It exists because someone labored, saved, planned, and invested. Land, by contrast, is not produced by anyone. It is the surface of the earth, the electromagnetic spectrum, mineral deposits, the fertility of soil, the flow of rivers, and the locations upon which human civilization is built. No human being manufactured the island of Manhattan. No entrepreneur conjured the oil beneath the Arabian Peninsula. No laborer constructed the harbor of San Francisco Bay.

This distinction is not merely taxonomic; it is profoundly moral. When a person builds a house, she has a clear and just claim to the value of that house. Her labor, her materials, her ingenuity produced it. But when the land beneath that house appreciates in value—because the city around it grew, because the government built a subway station nearby, because a million other people chose to live and work in the same metropolitan area—she has no comparable claim to that increase. She did not create it. The community created it.

The Lockean Foundation and Its Limits

Even John Locke, the philosopher most frequently invoked to defend private property, recognized that the right to appropriate from nature was conditional. In his Second Treatise of Government, Locke argued that a person could justly claim ownership of natural resources only when "there is enough, and as good, left in common for others." This is the famous Lockean proviso, and it is immediately obvious that it cannot be satisfied in any modern economy. There is no frontier. There is no unclaimed land of equivalent value available for the dispossessed. When all land is privately held and its rent is privately collected, latecomers to the economy—which is to say, every person born after the initial appropriation—are compelled to pay tribute to landowners simply to exist, to work, to live. They must pay rent not for any service rendered, not for any product created, but for the mere permission to occupy a portion of the Earth.

Thomas Paine recognized this injustice in his 1797 pamphlet Agrarian Justice, where he argued that "the earth, in its natural uncultivated state, was, and ever would have continued to be, the common property of the human race," and that every proprietor of land "owes to the community a ground-rent for the land which he holds." The full land value tax is simply the complete and systematic implementation of this principle.

The Injustice of Private Land Rent

Consider what land rent actually represents. A parcel of land in downtown Tokyo commands enormous rent not because the landowner has done anything extraordinary, but because twenty million people have collectively built a vast, complex, productive civilization around that spot. Every road, every rail line, every school, every hospital, every business, every cultural institution, every act of governance and policing and sanitation—the accumulated efforts of millions of people across generations—is capitalized into the value of that location. When a private landowner collects rent, she is siphoning off the value created by this collective endeavor. She is, in effect, charging the community for the privilege of accessing what the community itself has produced.

This is not entrepreneurship. This is not reward for risk or innovation. This is the extraction of wealth through the monopoly control of a resource that is fixed in supply and necessary for all human activity. Every human being requires land to stand on, to sleep on, to grow food on, to build a factory on. Land is not optional. It is the prerequisite for existence itself. To allow private individuals to collect rent on this prerequisite—rent they did not earn and could not have created—is to sanction a fundamental injustice at the base of the economic order.

The full land value tax rectifies this. By capturing 100% of the unimproved value of land for public use, it ensures that the value created by the community returns to the community. Landholders retain full ownership and use of their land. They retain full ownership of every improvement they make—every building, every garden, every fence. They lose only the ability to pocket the rental value that they never earned in the first place.

Part II: The Economic Case — Unmatched Efficiency

The Deadweight Loss of Conventional Taxes

Every introductory economics textbook teaches that taxes on productive activity create deadweight loss—a reduction in total economic output caused by the distortion of incentives. Income taxes discourage labor. Corporate taxes discourage investment. Sales taxes discourage consumption. Capital gains taxes discourage saving and risk-taking. Payroll taxes drive a wedge between what employers pay and what workers receive. Each of these taxes, however necessary they may seem, functions as a drag on the engine of economic production. They punish people for doing things we want them to do: working, building, trading, innovating.

The land value tax is unique among all possible taxes in that it creates zero deadweight loss. This is not a Georgist assertion alone; it is a conclusion reached by mainstream economists across the ideological spectrum. The reason is elementary: the supply of land is perfectly inelastic. No matter how high the tax on land value, the quantity of land does not change. You cannot produce more land in response to low taxes, and you cannot destroy land in response to high taxes. The land is simply there. A tax on its unimproved value therefore cannot distort any production decision, cannot discourage any productive activity, and cannot reduce the total output of the economy.

Milton Friedman—no friend of taxation in general—called the land value tax "the least bad tax." This was, if anything, an understatement born of his ideological reluctance to praise any tax too enthusiastically. The land value tax is not merely the least bad; it is positively good, because in addition to generating revenue without deadweight loss, it actively improves the allocation of resources.

The Incentive to Use Land Productively

Under the current system, a speculator can purchase a prime urban lot, leave it vacant, and simply wait for the surrounding community to increase its value. This is the practice of land speculation, and it is one of the most destructive and parasitic activities in any economy. The speculator contributes nothing. She builds nothing. She employs no one. She adds no product or service to the marketplace. She simply holds a scarce resource out of use, restricting supply, driving up rents and housing prices for everyone else, and pocketing the appreciation that the community's growth generates.

A 100% land value tax annihilates the incentive for such speculation. If the full rental value of land must be paid to the public treasury each year, there is no profit in holding land idle. The speculator must either put the land to its most productive use—building housing, opening a business, creating a park—or release it to someone who will. The result is an enormous unlocking of economic potential. Urban vacant lots become housing. Underutilized parcels become productive enterprises. The artificial scarcity of land, which drives housing crises in every major city on Earth, is broken.

Consider the staggering scale of the problem. In cities like London, San Francisco, Vancouver, Sydney, and Hong Kong, the price of housing has risen to levels that consume enormous shares of household income, not because of the cost of building homes—construction costs have remained relatively stable—but because of the cost of land. The land beneath a modest home in San Francisco can be worth more than the home itself, many times over. This inflated land value is pure rent-seeking. It represents wealth extracted by landowners from everyone else. A full land value tax would collapse speculative land prices toward zero (since the full annual rental value would be owed as tax), making land available at its true cost of use, dramatically reducing housing costs, and redirecting the vast sums currently consumed by mortgage interest and rent payments into productive investment, consumption, and saving.

The Elimination of Tax Distortions

Replacing all other taxes with a single tax on land value would unleash economic dynamism of a kind most people have never imagined. Consider the cumulative burden of the present tax system:

  • Income taxes discourage workers from seeking additional employment, accepting overtime, or pursuing education and skill development. They create a vast compliance bureaucracy and incentivize elaborate avoidance schemes.
  • Corporate taxes incentivize firms to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions, to underinvest in domestic production, and to structure transactions for tax efficiency rather than economic efficiency.
  • Sales and excise taxes are regressive, falling hardest on the poor, and distort consumption decisions.
  • Capital gains taxes discourage investment, punish successful risk-taking, and create lock-in effects where assets are held inefficiently to avoid realization events.
  • Payroll taxes increase the cost of employment, reducing hiring and suppressing wages.
  • Property taxes on improvements (as currently structured in most jurisdictions) actively punish people for building, renovating, and improving their property—the exact opposite of what a rational tax system should do.

Abolishing every one of these taxes and replacing them with the single land value tax removes every one of these distortions simultaneously. Workers keep every dollar they earn. Businesses keep every dollar of profit they generate through productive activity. Investors keep every gain from successful ventures. Consumers face no tax wedge on purchases. Employers face no surcharge for hiring. And property owners are rewarded, not penalized, for improving their buildings and land. The only thing taxed is the unearned, unproduced, community-generated value of location.

The result would be an economy of extraordinary vitality. The billions of hours currently spent on tax compliance, tax planning, and tax avoidance would be redirected to productive work. The enormous apparatus of the IRS and its equivalents worldwide could be reduced to a relatively modest land valuation and assessment administration. The efficiency of the land value tax is not a fringe position. It is grounded in the deepest results of economic theory. The Henry George Theorem, formalized by Joseph Stiglitz (a Nobel laureate in economics), demonstrates that under reasonable conditions, the aggregate land rent in an economy equals the aggregate expenditure on public goods. This remarkable result implies that a tax on land rent is not only sufficient to fund all public expenditures but is in fact the natural and optimal source of public revenue. Public investment increases land values; capturing those land values funds further public investment. The system is self-reinforcing, elegant, and complete.

William Vickrey, another Nobel laureate, was an outspoken advocate of land value taxation and site value rating. Paul Samuelson acknowledged that a tax on the "pure rent" of land was economically ideal. Simplicity of Administration

A 100% land value tax is radically simpler to administer than the labyrinthine tax codes that govern modern nations. Many jurisdictions already separately assess land and improvement values for property tax purposes; the transition would be an extension, not a revolution, in assessment practice.

Unlike income, which can be hidden in offshore accounts, shell companies, and complex financial structures, land cannot be hidden. It cannot be moved to the Cayman Islands. It cannot be disguised as something else. It sits in plain view, fixed and immovable, precisely where it has always been. This makes the land value tax perhaps the most evasion-proof tax ever conceived. The opportunities for fraud, avoidance, and arbitrage that plague income and corporate tax systems are virtually eliminated.

The land value tax is inherently progressive. Land ownership is far more concentrated than income or even financial wealth. A full land value tax falls most heavily on those who hold the greatest share of this most fundamental form of wealth. This progressivity is achieved without the complex system of brackets, deductions, credits, exemptions, phase-outs, and means-testing that characterizes modern income tax systems and that creates an entire industry of lobbyists, accountants, and lawyers devoted to manipulating the code. Perhaps the most profound governance benefit of the single tax is its effect on political corruption and rent-seeking. Every exemption, deduction, credit, and favorable rate represents a prize worth millions or billions of dollars to its beneficiaries, and these beneficiaries spend lavishly to obtain and defend their privileges. The result is a tax code that is not merely complex but actively rigged—a system in which the politically connected pay less and the politically powerless pay more.

A single tax on land value offers no such opportunities. There are no loopholes to create, no exemptions to lobby for, no rates to differentiate. The tax base is objective, visible, and uniform. No tax is assessed with perfect precision; the relevant question is whether land value can be assessed with sufficient accuracy to be administered fairly, and the evidence overwhelmingly shows that it can.

Moreover, the assessment of land value benefits from the transparency of real estate markets. Land sales, building permits, and rental data are publicly recorded. "Land rents are insufficient to fund modern government."

When one includes the full range of natural resource rents, spectrum rents, and other returns to nature and location, the aggregate "Georgist tax base" is enormous.

Furthermore, the replacement of all other taxes would itself expand the economy substantially, increasing land values and thus land tax revenue. The elimination of deadweight loss from income, corporate, and sales taxes would boost production, raise wages, increase trade, and drive up the demand for well-located land. The Henry George Theorem provides theoretical support for the proposition that optimal public goods provision generates sufficient land rent to fund itself.

It is also worth noting that a society committed to the single tax might reasonably revisit the appropriate level of government spending. Much of current government expenditure is devoted to ameliorating problems—poverty, housing unaffordability, unemployment, regional inequality—that the land value tax would substantially reduce or eliminate. A more efficient economy with fairer distribution would require less remedial spending.

"It is politically impossible."

Political difficulty is not a moral or economic argument. Every great reform in history—the abolition of slavery, universal suffrage, the end of feudal land tenure—was once deemed politically impossible. The land value tax faces political opposition precisely because it threatens the interests of the most powerful constituency in any economy: those who own the most valuable land. Banks that hold mortgages, real estate developers who profit from speculation, wealthy landowners who benefit from appreciation—these are formidable opponents. The political case for the land value tax must be built through education, demonstration, and incremental implementation. Each success builds the case for broader adoption.

The case for the 100% land value tax as the sole source of public revenue is not merely strong; it is, upon honest examination, overwhelming. It rests on the unassailable moral principle that what no one created belongs to everyone. It is supported by the most rigorous economic analysis available, endorsed by Nobel laureates and economists across the spectrum. And it is long past time that we had the courage to implement it.

Georgist Land Value Tax: Claimed Benefits and Reasoning

Core Premise

Georgist philosophy, originating with Henry George's Progress and Poverty (1879), draws a distinction between:

  • Land (and natural resources) — not produced by human effort, fixed in supply
  • Improvements — buildings, infrastructure, and other products of labor and investment

The central argument is that land value arises from community presence, public investment, and natural advantages rather than from any action by the landowner, and therefore that this value is the most appropriate base for public revenue.

Claimed Economic Benefits

Efficiency Arguments

  • No deadweight loss (in theory): Because the supply of land is fixed, taxing its unimproved value would not reduce the quantity available, unlike taxes on labor, sales, or capital which can discourage the taxed activity. This point is acknowledged even by many economists outside the Georgist tradition, dating back to David Ricardo and endorsed by figures like Milton Friedman, who called it "the least bad tax."
  • Discourages speculation: Holding idle or underused land becomes costly, since the tax must be paid regardless of whether the land is developed. This would theoretically push land into productive use.
  • Removes drag on productive activity: By replacing taxes on income, sales, and capital gains, the system would stop penalizing work, investment, saving, and trade.

Development and Land Use

  • Encourages optimal use of land: Since improvements are untaxed, there is a direct incentive to develop land to its highest productive use. Building a factory or apartment building would not increase one's tax burden.
  • Reduces urban blight and sprawl: Vacant lots in valuable urban areas would become expensive to hold, incentivizing development in already-serviced areas rather than pushing outward to cheaper undeveloped land.

Distributional Arguments

  • Captures publicly created value: When a government builds a transit line and nearby land values rise, currently that windfall goes to private landowners. A land value tax would return that publicly generated value to the public.
  • Addresses inequality rooted in land ownership: George argued that poverty persists alongside progress because landowners capture increasing shares of economic growth through rising rents, without contributing to that growth.
  • Cannot be passed on to tenants (in theory): Since the tax does not change the supply or demand for land, standard economic analysis suggests the burden falls entirely on landowners rather than being shifted to renters through higher rents. The argument is that rents are already set at whatever the market will bear; the tax merely determines how much of that rent the owner keeps versus pays in tax.

Simplicity and Transparency

  • Hard to evade: Land cannot be hidden, moved offshore, or concealed in shell companies the way income or financial assets can be.
  • Relatively straightforward to assess: While land valuation has challenges, the physical presence of land makes it more visible than many other tax bases.
  • Replaces a complex web of taxes: A single tax would theoretically eliminate the administrative burden of income taxes, payroll taxes, corporate taxes, sales taxes, and various other levies.

Philosophical and Moral Arguments

  • Self-ownership principle: People should own the full fruits of their labor. Taxing wages and exchange is seen as a partial claim on someone's effort, while taxing land value is claiming something no individual created.
  • Common inheritance: Land and natural resources existed before any person and are argued to be the common heritage of all people. Private appropriation of land rent is viewed as unjust enrichment at the community's expense.
  • Lockean proviso: John Locke argued that private appropriation of nature is justified only when "enough and as good" is left for others. George argued this condition is routinely violated, and a land value tax serves as compensation.

How It Would Supposedly Work as a Sole Revenue Source

Georgists argue that aggregate land rent in developed economies is large enough — potentially sufficient to fund government operations — though this is one of the more contested empirical claims. Estimates of total land rent as a share of GDP vary significantly depending on methodology and definitions.

Important Caveats

It is worth noting that these are the arguments made by proponents. Significant objections and practical challenges exist:

  • Assessment difficulties: Separating land value from improvement value is complex in practice.
  • Revenue sufficiency: Whether land rents alone could fund modern government budgets is debated.
  • Transition disruption: Current landowners would face potentially dramatic losses in asset values.
  • Political feasibility: Concentrated opposition from landowners versus diffuse benefits.
  • Edge cases: Treatment of agricultural land, natural resources, and varying local conditions adds complexity.

Georgist ideas have influenced real-world policy in partial forms — notably in parts of Pennsylvania, Denmark, Estonia, Singapore, and Hong Kong — but no jurisdiction has implemented a full 100% land value tax as its sole revenue source.

A tax on its unimproved value causes no distortion, no disincentive, no drag on the productive economy.

A moral economy at last. Think about what our current tax system tells people. It says: if you work hard, we will take a share of your earnings. If you build a factory, we will tax it. If you improve your property, we will raise your assessment. But if you sit on a piece of land and do nothing — if you contribute nothing — we will let you grow rich on the efforts of the community around you.

All that is lacking is the political will. All that is lacking is the courage to challenge the most powerful vested interest in human history — the interest of those who profit from the monopolization of the Earth itself.

His answer was land monopoly. His solution was the public capture of land rent.

Nearly 150 years later, the question is more urgent than ever. Our cities are unaffordable. Our workers are overtaxed. Our economy is strangled by speculation. Our public finances are built on a foundation of taxes that punish everything we want more of — work, investment, creativity — while leaving untaxed the one thing we should be capturing: the value of our common Earth.

The solution is before us. It has always been before us. Written in the logic of economics. Written in the principles of justice. Written in the self-evident truth that the Earth belongs — equally, inalienably, and forever — to all of the people who walk upon it.

Let us, at last, have the courage to act on what we know to be true.

Let us tax the land. All of it.

Let us free labor, free enterprise, free the human spirit from the burden of unjust taxation.

Let us build, at last, an economy worthy of a free people standing on common ground.

Introduction to Georgism and the Land Value Tax

Georgism is an economic philosophy named after Henry George, an American political economist and journalist from the late 19th century. Central to Georgist thought is the belief that while individuals should own the value they create through their labor and capital investment, the economic value derived from land (including natural resources and opportunities) should belong equally to all members of society.

A key policy proposal of Georgism is the implementation of a 100% tax on unimproved land value, commonly known as the land value tax (LVT). This tax would apply solely to the intrinsic value of the land itself, excluding any enhancements or developments made upon it, such as buildings, crops, or other improvements. The revenue generated from this tax would serve as the primary—or sole—source of public funding, replacing other forms of taxation.

Supposed Benefits and Reasons for Adopting a 100% Land Value Tax

  1. Promotes Efficient Land Use

    • Discourages Land Speculation: Taxing the unimproved value of land reduces the incentive to hold land purely for speculative purposes. Landowners are motivated to either put the land to productive use or release it to those who will, leading to more optimal allocation of land resources.

    • Encourages Development: With the cost of holding undeveloped or underused land increased, owners are incentivized to develop properties to generate income to cover the tax, fostering economic activity and urban development.

  2. Economic Efficiency

    • Non-Distortionary Taxation: Since the supply of land is fixed—it cannot be hidden, moved, or increased—a tax on land value does not distort economic behavior in the way taxes on labor or capital might. Individuals and businesses continue to work and invest without the disincentive effect of additional taxes on their productive efforts.

    • Minimizes Deadweight Loss: Traditional taxes can create deadweight losses by discouraging production or consumption. A land value tax minimizes these losses because it does not reduce the quantity of land available or alter its intrinsic value.

  3. Ensures Fair Distribution of Wealth

    • Captures Unearned Income (Economic Rent): Land value often increases due to societal factors—such as infrastructure development, population growth, or community investments—rather than the actions of the individual landowner. Taxing this unearned increment ensures that the community benefits from value it collectively helped create.

    • Reduces Income Inequality: Concentration of land ownership can lead to significant wealth disparities. By redistributing the economic rent from land, a land value tax can help mitigate wealth inequality.

  4. Simplifies the Tax System

    • Single Tax Principle: Replacing multiple forms of taxation (income, sales, property taxes on buildings, etc.) with a single land value tax simplifies the tax system. It reduces administrative costs for both the government and taxpayers and makes compliance easier.

    • Transparency and Predictability: Land valuations are generally stable and transparent, making tax assessments straightforward and predictable.

  5. Stimulates Economic Growth

    • Encourages Investment and Production: Without taxes on labor, capital gains, or business profits, individuals and companies are more likely to invest, produce, and innovate, driving economic growth.

    • Boosts Employment: Increased investment and development activities can lead to job creation across various sectors, reducing unemployment.

  6. Eliminates Tax Evasion and Avoidance

    • Immobility of Land: Land cannot be relocated to offshore tax havens or concealed, making it a reliable tax base. This reduces opportunities for tax evasion and increases the efficiency of tax collection.

  7. Addresses Urban Sprawl and Environmental Concerns

    • Promotes Sustainable Development: Efficient land use reduces the need for urban sprawl, preserving natural habitats and reducing environmental degradation.

    • Encourages Infill Development: By making it costly to hold undeveloped urban land, a land value tax encourages development within existing urban areas, optimizing infrastructure use and reducing the environmental impact of new developments.

  8. Enhances Housing Affordability

    • Reduces Land Hoarding: Owners of vacant or underutilized land are incentivized to develop or sell, increasing the supply of available land for housing, which can help lower housing costs.

    • Stabilizes Real Estate Markets: By limiting speculative land price inflation, housing markets become more stable and affordable over time.

  9. Aligns with the Principle of Natural Rights

    • Equal Access to Natural Opportunities: Georgism holds that natural resources and opportunities should be accessible to all. A land value tax operationalizes this principle by sharing the economic benefits derived from land among the entire community.

  10. Provides Adequate Public Revenue

    • Stable Revenue Source: Land values tend to be stable or appreciate over time, providing a consistent and potentially growing revenue stream for public expenditures.

    • Funding Public Goods and Services: The revenue collected can be used to fund infrastructure, education, healthcare, and other public services, benefiting society as a whole.

Conclusion

Adopting a 100% tax on unimproved land value as the sole source of public revenue is proposed by Georgists as a means to create a more equitable, efficient, and prosperous society. By taxing the unearned economic rent of land, the government can eliminate less efficient and more distortionary taxes on labor and capital, promoting productive economic activity. This approach is intended to ensure that the benefits of natural resources and societal progress are shared among all members of the community, addressing issues of wealth inequality and social justice. Additionally, it streamlines the tax system, reduces opportunities for tax evasion, and aligns individual incentives with the collective good, fostering sustainable development and long-term economic growth.
